content: Medication reconciliation is a structured process aimed at obtaining a comprehensive and accurate list of a patient’s current home medications. This includes the medication name, dosage, frequency, and route of administration. The process involves comparing this list to the medications ordered at the time of admission, transfer, or discharge to identify and resolve any discrepancies. The primary goal of medication reconciliation is to prevent medication errors. Older adults often face challenges in accurately recalling their medications, which can complicate the process. To address this, healthcare providers may establish a Best Possible Medication History (BPMH) to ensure accuracy. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) defines medication reconciliation as the process of creating the most accurate list possible of all medications a patient is taking. Similarly, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) describe it as identifying the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking. The Joint Commission emphasizes that a clinician compares the medications a patient should be using (and is actually using) to the new medications ordered and resolves any discrepancies. Epidemiology of Medication Reconciliation Errors Frequency of Reconciliation Errors In inpatient settings, medication error rates vary significantly: Discrepancies have been reported in 17%, 44%, 46%, and 60% of cases. Inappropriate medication choices, as identified by STOPP/START criteria, occur in 48% of cases. A related issue, though not classified as an error, is the increase in medication intensity at the time of hospital discharge. In outpatient settings, medication error rates are even higher: Discrepancies have been reported in 44%, 76%, 83%, and 88% of cases. Specific errors in inpatient settings include: Discrepancies with discharge summaries: 34% Duplicate medications: 23% Extraneous medications: 14% Medications prescribed by indication or disease: 25% Omission of medications: 17% Frequency of Harm from Reconciliation Errors Studies have reported varying rates of complications resulting from medication errors. However, it remains unclear how many of these issues could be avoided through successful medication reconciliation. In one study involving 851 patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or congestive heart failure (CHF), 8% of patients experienced clinically significant medication errors, with 8% of these being life-threatening and 7% classified as potential adverse events. In another study of 510 hematology/oncology patients attending infusion center appointments without a provider visit, student pharmacists conducted medication reconciliation. They found: 88% of patients had at least one discrepancy in their medication history, which was corrected in the electronic medical record (EMR). 4% of patients had medication-related problems, including drug-drug interactions, untreated indications, adverse drug reactions, and untreated conditions. Methods for Identifying Medication Problems Criteria for Determining Medication Problems One proposed metric is the number of unintentional medication discrepancies per patient. This measure requires a trained pharmacist to assess discrepancies against a gold standard. The authors of this measure suggest sampling 25 patients per month, or approximately one patient per weekday. However, challenges with this approach include unclear criteria used by pharmacists and the inability to automate or routinely measure this during patient care. In clinical practice, physicians may have less than a minute to discuss medications with patients. Specific Criteria A study conducted at the Washington DC VA proposed specific criteria for medication reconciliation. Internal medicine residents participated in bi-monthly educational sessions led by faculty or chief residents, focusing on the accuracy of discharge medication reconciliation. The criteria included: Identification of duplicate medications Identification of extraneous medications (also referred to as one-time, post-acute, or time-limited medications in other studies) Discrepancies from discharge summaries Omission of medications Grouping medications by indication or disease While some criteria showed significant improvement after intervention, the reliability of these results was not tested. Another study at National Jewish Health in Denver, which serves patients with respiratory and related diseases, assessed medication reconciliation performance by comparing patients’ medication lists at clinical transition points. The study demonstrated improvement in outpatient settings but highlighted the need for sustainable and valid measures. Significant improvements were noted in addressing missing doses and their frequencies. Patients were also provided with medication safety handouts containing their updated medication lists. However, compliance remained a limiting factor due to redundancy in the process and poor buy-in from participants. Role of Patient Engagement and Understanding Elderly patients often struggle to understand changes in their medications. Low health literacy is strongly associated with medication discrepancies. Role of Regional Health Information Exchanges The use of data from regional health information exchanges has been advocated to improve medication reconciliation. However, the clinical benefit of using such exchanges remains unproven. A randomized controlled trial found no reduction in adverse drug reactions with the use of health information exchanges. Quality Measures Medication reconciliation is a quality measure for both the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA). Public Reporting Medication reconciliation is included in the CMS Electronic Health Record (EHR) Incentive Programs for Meaningful Use Stage 1 and the 2017 Modified Stage 2 Meaningful Use Program Requirements. Interventions to Promote Successful Medication Reconciliation Medication reconciliation, as a standalone intervention, may not be effective. Conducting medication reconciliation at the time of hospital discharge alone is insufficient to prevent hospital readmissions, although it may reduce subsequent emergency department usage. When medication reconciliation is combined with follow-up phone calls, evidence of benefit regarding hospital re-utilization after discharge is conflicting. Some trials report benefits, while others do not. Studies suggest that benefits are more likely when multiple, scripted phone calls are made, and patients are encouraged to bring their medications to the phone. Multi-factorial interventions that include medication reconciliation may reduce hospital readmissions.
